masterclasses.description: Performer can only preform as well as he can hear. A composer can only compose what he can think up.

practices.title: Comments
practices.description: Comments on the masterclass.
practices.text:
Perfect pitch sounds so long good until you take your pace to practice it. It's always hard to learn something new. It takes time and energy.

[b]Keywords[/b]
Performer can only preform as well as he can hear. A composer can only compose what he can think up. And you can only think up what your ear can comprehend, what your ear can grasp. You can only appreciate and enjoy whatever your own perception and awareness allows you to enjoy. It is all dependent on your own musical awareness. Perfect pitch is the color in music (black and white TV example). Its a delicate perception which opens up the ear in all area of music. Its something which is already in our ear.

practices.text:
I'm a Double bass player. Now I remembered that I couldn't decide on which instrument to practice the exercises. He says that you should be on your live, own instrument but on the other hand that people with no musical experience can both learn perfect pitch. I'm a [code]python[/code] programming hobbyist and I will try to write all the practices.

[b]Keywords[/b]
Relative and perfect pitch are both important.
Relative pitch help us to say that the chord is [i]dominant:9[/i] and perfect pitch is helping us to hear that it is on tone [b]d[/b].
Absolute means non changing. [b]A[/b] has always the same sound. It is absolute.

[b]Different levels:[/b]
[ul]color awareness
color discrimination (12 chromatic pitch colors) - quality of sound
[/ul]

[b]Exercise[/b]
o to your own instrument and have a listen, here for yourself that this color sounds do exist.

practices.title: Comments
practices.description: Comments on the masterclass.
practices.text:
About the tones. I didn't hear color as he said but I started to hear tones in space. I'm aware now that each tone has its own place in space.

p.s. don't force yourself.

[b]Keywords[/b]
We learn to distinguish these colors between the very fine variations that there are the tones.
But they become very clear. We get to know this sound colors.
We have to get it out of that habit (listening horizontally) and into the habit of listening inside the tones.
Composers have used variates keys and chords in different ways for different reasons even unconsciously.
Absolute pitch training is a effortless training. What we don't wanna do is practice perfect pitch training with this idea that your gonna get in there and force your ear and wipe it and shape. If you strain the ear will not hear. Ear will only feel when it feels comfortable and relaxed and you just let it listen.
As we do listen our color discrimination grows.

3. level of perfect pitch: Refined color discrimination (you can tell if tone is sharp or flat to standard concert pitch)

Some people think if you have perfect pitch that you have mental barometer in your brain witch just register [i]BOING[/i] and tells you exactly how high or low the pitch is.

Firstly you can here this colors on your own instrument, but as soon as somebody plays it on some other instrument we have no idea, your completely lost. Now this is a common experience. This is perfect pitch but it's just one level of it. We can refine our hearing even more so that we can here it on all instruments. This would be called [b]Universal color discrimination[/b]. When the ear can here this colors clearly and recognized them in all the universal variety of pitches whether is our own instrument on piano, guitar, oboe, violin, bassoon, bells, little glasses of water, whistle or birds, voices.
The ear has to learn the distinction between pitch colors (pitch itself) and tone color (of the instrument). Spectral discrimination.
It's a human perception.

4. level: aural recall (not raw memorising, it's hearing a color)

When you want to sing Ab you don't judge how high or low the tone is. What you do you think up is the color sound. What does it sounds like.

[b]Exercise[/b]
[ul]Try F# ( 1 3 5 8 ) and Eb chords and listen to the difference. Were are not listening to a clear difference, it's a saddle thing. It's a feeling that when you play the F# chord and you move to the Eb something has changed.
Listen a little more for yourself.
Read you perfect pitch handbook.
Another listen to the tones. Listen gently and easily to the tones.
[/ul]

masterclasses.title: Masterclass 5
masterclasses.description: Just follow the method. Step by step.

practices.title: Listen to masterclass
practices.description: Audio book player. Here you will listen to David Lucas Burge audio book.

practices.title: Comments
practices.description: Comments on the masterclass.
practices.text:
[b]Keywords[/b]
[ul][i]Phase 1[/i] - prep the ear
[i]Phase 2[/i] - all the color become clear at the same time.
[i]Phase 3[/i] - polish it even more[/ul]

Were in a big class room.
The foundation on music is hearing.
You just follow the method. Step by step.
When you do know how to listen and progress step by step it becomes simplified.
You need to take the time to listen. You can't rush it.
Listen to each session all the way through including the parts that may on may not apply to you.

You go to the next masterclass after you have successfully finished all exercises.

What instrument to use.
The result will be faster if you use the instrument you play most. 
The instrument that your ear is most familiar with.
You can use that training on any instrument. But you have to get used to the sound first.
You can't do chords on a flute. But you can have flute chords on synthesiser.
Use that one sound for all your ear training practice all the way up until we get to phase 3.
Relative pitch is a different story.

We wanna do about two octave bellow middle C and two octave above.
Start up using a medium range of tones on your instrument at first.

Some of the exercises that were going to do are hearing exercises and some are singing exercises.
When your doing a hearing exercises you just listen, you don't sing the tone. We don't wanna start judging pitches with our voice. We wanna learn the pitch by hearing.

Were going to divide our exercises into three main categories:

[ol]solo keyboards
solo guitar
teams of two (additional drill methods)[/ol]

Ear training meditation technique.
It is important to clearly understand the theory behind perfect pitch and how perfect pitch becomes cultured into the ear.
We want to listen to each masterclasse one at the time. We never wanna do more then one masterclass in a day.
Take as long as you need to practice the exercises. Maybe you'll need even three weeks on one particular homework assignment from a masterclass.
We don't rush ourself. We go at our own pace.
We don't wanna be left behind on any step. This is a crucial secret to perfect pitch development.
We don't practice for a long time each day. The short ear training session is all it takes. Actually your ear will go faster if you just give it a short session but you do it daily.

For our solo practises we just wanna listen for about 10 or 15 minutes. Don't think you have to go on, and on, and on. Sometimes when people train their ear to much then they find they can't hear anything. Has this ever happen to you? It's like you can take a shower for 10 minutes or 30 minutes. But 10 minutes is plane.

The same for teams.
Progress to the next masterclass when you feel ready. And if by chance you ever get stuck anywhere in your practice....

[b]Exercise - Phase 1 - Color hearing:[/b]

[b]Solo keyboards[/b]
Reach to your keyboard and play any two white tones that are separated by one white tone like E and G. Were just using the white tones only. Now we listen carefully to sound of these two tones. Listen individually so that you can hear each of the two tones. Usually we may only hear the top tone. So we have to listen little more closely to the bottom tone. Let your ear get inside to hear the bottom tone as well as the top tone. Now to prove that you really are hearing these tones we sing them (from the bottom up). When you can sing the tones then you have proved that you really have heard both tones. You didn't just hear the top one. If you can't hear the bottom tone than play it. Listen to it separately. Then play the two tones together again and see if you can now hear the bottom tone. Just work with your ear like this. Take your time. Work with this drill until you can any two tones separate by one white tone. You don't have to name the pitch. Were just singing the tones.

[b]Solo guitar[/b]
Just play a string at random and just try to tell which it is. Learn your string.

[b]Solo instrumentalist[/b]
Evan easter. Just listen carefully to C and D (regardless of your instrument, if your Bb instrument your C will sound Bb) and sing them very concisely like a meditation. Here is how we do it. Listen to C on your instrument. Gently hear the tone. Let it sock into your ear. Then here the pitch in your own mind. Imagine the pitch then sing the pitch (Laaa) and then sing the pitch again. Were just using C and D right now. We don't have to worry about any other tones. And were using it on our own instrument.

Have fun!

masterclasses.title: Masterclass 6
masterclasses.description: The little experience of joy or happiness as an experience of the depth of perception which music has to offer.

practices.title: Listen to masterclass
practices.description: Audio book player. Here you will listen to David Lucas Burge audio book.

practices.title: Comments
practices.description: Comments on the masterclass.
practices.text:
[b]Keywords[/b]
The little experiance of joy or happynes as an experiance of the depth of perception which music has to offer.

[b]Unlocking tehnique with major and minor secodns.[/b]
We go deeper into our color tehnique exercisses. Right now were getting our ear to zoom in on our tones to unlock them. So that were able to hear each tone discretly. Now were gana make it a little trickier. Were ganna do the same things with major and minor seconds.

[i]Solo keyboards[/i]
[ol]1. Major and minor seconds (harmonicly, only white tones). And were singing it from the bottom up (melodicly).
A little bit of an ear teaser for you to sort out the top tone from the bottom tone. As you continue they clearify. When you can sing it then your ear has open up that much more.
2. Unlock any two tones using one hand only (octave) and sing them from the bottom up.
3. Unlock wide tones. This means we play our tones wide. We reach out with two hands and play tones that are more spaced out ( bigger then one octave ) and we sing them from the bottom up. The octave is not important. Were listening them in whatever the octave they are and were singing them in what ever range voice we can sing them
[/ol]

[i]Last unlocking solo drills.[/i]
[ol]4. Do three tones close. Reach out play any three tones one handed. We listen , we unlock the sounds with our ears so we here each note discretly and then we sing them from the bottom up. And we check ourselfs.
5. Three tones wide. Reach out, play two tones in one hand and one tone in the other hand.
[/ol]

Remember, go slow on this drills. We listen with great intrest. Remember, its the listening that is opening our ear. So evan if we can do this drill easily we still need to take time to listen. This is the key to development of perfect pitch. If you for example can't hear the middle tone in drill 4. Listen again, and play separatly. And then play the problem chord again. Allow you ear to relax. Don't strain or force you ear in any way. Any time you find that a chord is trickie it just go to proof that you ear was not hearing thise things all along. The ear was sleeping. It just shows we need ear traning. Keep working on our ear and youl find that it will cooperate and it will begin to hear this things. The magic formula is: keep listening, keep listening, keep listening and listen gently.

[b]Meditation tehnique for this session[/b]
[i]All instrumentalist[/i]
We play a tone, we think of it, and we sing it again.
We think the tone before we sing it. This is the diference.
We always correct our mistakes. We never just move on. We always take the time to hear the wrong note and the right note.
Do it like a meditation. Slow, queit, easy and relaxed.

[i]Solo guitar[/i]
The same as solo keyboards.

We'll considure to have pass that drill when we can do one verification round.
A verification round means that you pass tweny examples in a row all corectly without a mistake.
If you didn't do it right you have to correct your error. If you make a mistake you have to go all over again. When you do one verification round then you have masterd this drill.
15 minutes a day on the solo drills until your confortable with them.

[i]Team drills[/i]
Melodic and Harmonic pitch indentification. C and D exacept guitarist. Guitarist A and B(H).
[ul]1. One person plays evan C or D and the other person names it. One verification round.
2. Were ganna play two tones together. We indetify from the bottom up. Close or wide. When we play melodicly we always indentifie in the order that they were played.
[/ul]
Don't skip a drill if you think that they are easy.

practices.title: Listen to masterclass
practices.description: Audio book player. Here you will listen to David Lucas Burge audio book.

practices.title: Comments
practices.description: Comments on the masterclass.
practices.text:
[b]Keywords[/b]
You with perfect pitch will be able to play far more better by ear then you without.
Exercise

[i]Solo keyboard[/i]
[ul]Reach out and play any white tone anywhere on the keyboard and name it. We're using the C major scale so you would know the tones by relative pitch. At this point we don't have full color discrimination. So the ear needs something to latch on to in order to know the tone. And thats fine if you know the tone by relative pitch. Just name the pitch. Don't be to hasty with your pitch naming. Go slowly. Listen to the tone. Take an interest in the tone. Allow a tone to soak for a moment. Something else is happening inside. If you get it wrong then pause. Listen to both tones. And you can even listen to it in a relationship to the C. One verification round.[/ul]

[i]Solo guitars[/i]
Two stings at a time and unlock them by ear. From the bottom up. Reach out and play any two open strings and indentify them. Don't worry about finger knowlidge.

[i]Meditation[/i]
[ul]C, D and E. When ever we seat to practice we think of a C and sing it. We need to correct our error.[/ul]

[i]Team players[/i]
C, D and E. Harmonic and melodic pitch indentification.
[ul]Single. Single tone pitch nameing drill.
Melodic doubles.
Harmonic doubles.[/ul]

Correct the error. This is where the ear traning comes in. We need to get listening benefit. We listen again to open more and more.
Sing a C and check. Sing a E. Take you timer and be very present in the moment. No verification round.

practices.title: Coverage, source status and manual guitar tasks
practices.description: Read coverage, adaptations and manual capo instructions.
practices.text:
Coverage: ascending, descending and strict harmonic white-third naming; C/D/E/F and guitar A/B/C#/D recall meditation; six team naming variants; opening C/A recall. The app supplies a digital partner, a MIDI 36–84 range and distinct MIDI-note doubles; these are app choices, not source prescriptions. Harmonic thirds may be rocked for assistance, but the verification round requires strict simultaneous presentation. Work slowly; naming exercises are listening, not singing.

Uncertainty: the curriculum is text-supported and audio-unverified. Exact register, timing, singing tolerance, repeat-note policy and randomization distribution are not source-defined. Keyboard answers check names, not microphone performance; singing/recall is self-reported.

Manual guitar assignments (master-class-08-p04 and master-class-08-p05): capo so the E string sounds F, determine the new sounding pitch of every string, then name random single strings followed by two strings together. Use the new pitch names, not original string names. Work until familiar; no verification round. Once comfortable, repeat with E sounding A. The source does not enumerate the full shifted tuning or prescribe a fret number here; none is invented. These physical string-recognition tasks are not generated by the app.

practices.title: Coverage, source status and app adaptations
practices.description: Read source coverage, completion rules, adaptations and uncertainties.
practices.text:
All 12 source practices are individually exposed: white sixths (not thirds), two five-tone recall collections, A-major cue naming and both team collections.

Source status: text_supported_audio_unverified; source windows are evidence references, not independently checked audio. MIDI 36–84, synthesized playback, keyboard entry and random sampling are app adaptations, not source register, voicing, timing or distribution requirements. Naming means listen and name, not sing. Recall means imagine before reference playback, sing, check and self-report; no numeric singing tolerance or octave-specific vocal threshold is invented. Meditation retains the inherited twenty-correct rule: this lesson continues/adds tones without restating its round count.

Cue drills return to the chord before every chromatic target and require two separately tracked rounds of twenty consecutive correct answers, not forty uninterrupted. A wrong answer restarts the current round. The app cue is a synthesized close-position triad, not a claim to reproduce a physical guitar voicing. Distinct examples exclude exact repeated MIDI notes but allow octave duplicates; source repeat policy and exact range are unspecified. Harmonic naming is bottom-up; right pitch classes in the wrong order receive a reordering hint rather than an immediate wrong-answer reset.

White sixths require explicit confirmation of comfort/familiarity after twenty consecutive correct examples; counting alone does not pass. Loose harmonic sixths may be used as assistance before strict simultaneous verification. The source permits any A-major voicing and demonstrates A/E/A/C#/E; the app A3/C#4/E4 triad is an adaptation, not that demonstration or a required guitar shape.

practices.title: Coverage, source status and app adaptations
practices.description: Read source coverage, completion rules, adaptations and uncertainties.
practices.text:
All 25 source practices are individually exposed: white seconds, fifths, fourths and sevenths; B-major cue naming; two six-tone recall collections; and both team collections including triples.

Source status: text_supported_audio_unverified; source windows are evidence references, not independently checked audio. MIDI 36–84, synthesized playback, keyboard entry and random sampling are app adaptations, not source register, voicing, timing or distribution requirements. Naming means listen and name, not sing. Recall means imagine before reference playback, sing, check and self-report; no numeric singing tolerance or octave-specific vocal threshold is invented. Meditation retains the inherited twenty-correct rule: this lesson continues/adds tones without restating its round count.

Cue drills return to the chord before every chromatic target and require two separately tracked rounds of twenty consecutive correct answers, not forty uninterrupted. A wrong answer restarts the current round. The app cue is a synthesized close-position triad, not a claim to reproduce a physical guitar voicing. Distinct examples exclude exact repeated MIDI notes but allow octave duplicates; source repeat policy and exact range are unspecified. Harmonic naming is bottom-up; right pitch classes in the wrong order receive a reordering hint rather than an immediate wrong-answer reset.

White fifths include B–F; interval quality is not the naming task. No extra compulsory sequence between interval families is invented. Harmonic team examples require simultaneous-tone capability; source single-tone instrumentalists may omit them. The digital partner can sound simultaneous tones, but does not simulate physical guitar technique. No B-major voicing is specified in the source; B3/D#4/F#4 is solely the app cue.

practices.title: Coverage, source status and app adaptations
practices.description: Read exact coverage, source limitations, manual/deferred status and completion rules.
practices.text:
All 26 source assignments are individually exposed: 22 executable formulas (p01–p22) and four manual-guidance entries (p23–p26), plus player 0 and comments 1, for 28 practices total. White doubles allow close as well as wide spacing; their span is unrestricted within MIDI 36–84. One-hand white triples use a disclosed maximum of 12 semitones, an app approximation rather than a universal physical hand limit. Two-hand triples use span 0–48: no mandatory wide cutoff is stated.

The A-string cue is synthesized MIDI 45, not a recording or verification of a real guitar string. C#-major [61,65,68] and D#-major [63,67,70] follow the transcript names, which remain uncertain pending audio review; these close-position app voicings are not prescribed guitar voicings. Each cue precedes every new chromatic target; two rounds of twenty are inherited from the preceding assignment, not restated here.

Meditation includes the complete C-major collection including B, or the complete A-major collection including G#. Imagine the named tone before reference playback, sing, check and self-report; no microphone grading, cents tolerance or octave-specific vocal threshold is claimed. Team collections retain source counts: melodic one round, harmonic doubles/triples two rounds. Each round needs twenty consecutive correct examples; an error resets only the current round. Harmonic naming is bottom-up and allows a right-pitches/wrong-order reordering hint.

Manual long/short tone variations allow unlimited identification time; no seconds are specified. Constant-speed practice continues without stopping for errors; no numerical BPM is recoverable from the text. Subsequent ordinary instrument playing has no minimum duration. A manual acknowledgement records only that guidance was reviewed/practised, not a verification round or mastery.

Source status: text_supported_audio_unverified. Source windows and quotes are evidence references, not independently verified audio. MIDI 36–84, random sampling, synthesized playback and keyboard entry are app adaptations, not source timing, distribution, register or voicing requirements. Distinct excludes exact repeated MIDI notes but permits octave duplicates; source repeat policy is unspecified. Simultaneous-tone assignments require an appropriate instrument; the continued single-tone-instrument accommodation permits omitting harmonic examples. Digital playback does not establish physical one-/two-hand technique or a universal hand-span model.

practices.description: Aural recall and conscious singing. Choose a tone, imagine its sound first, sing it, then check it on the instrument. Imagine before sounding, sing, check and self-report; no automatic singing verification. Complete 1 separately tracked round(s) of twenty consecutive correct examples; an error resets the current round. App adaptation: MIDI 36–84 is a finite synthesized playback range, not a source-assigned register or octave-specific vocal requirement. App adaptation: synthesized playback and keyboard note-name entry replace instrument/partner actions; naming is listening and naming, not singing. App adaptation: distinct selects different absolute MIDI notes, allows octave duplicates of pitch classes, and excludes exact repeated notes within an example. Source repeat-note policy and randomization distribution are unspecified. App adaptation: physical one-/two-hand placement, fingering, hand reach and guitar technique are not assessed or simulated. A numeric span does not guarantee an individual can physically play an example; use a comfortable reach on the real instrument. App adaptation: show a named target silently; imagine first, sing, then play the reference and self-report accuracy. No microphone verification, numeric singing tolerance or octave-specific vocal pass threshold is implemented.

practices.title: Coverage, source status and app adaptations
practices.description: Read exact coverage, source limitations, manual/deferred status and completion rules.
practices.text:
All 28 source assignments are individually exposed: 18 executable formulas (p01–p14 and p25–p28), five manual-guidance transposing-instrument entries (p15–p19), and five deferred A-based team-guitar entries (p20–p24). With player 0 and comments 1 there are 30 practices total. The black-key naming formulas use only pitch classes 1,3,6,8,10; do not mix white keys into this assignment. Source spellings C#, F#, Eb, Ab, Bb permit enharmonic alternatives.

One-hand work uses a maximum span of 12 semitones as an app approximation, not a universal physical hand limit. The wide harmonic double minimum of 13 follows the preceding wide-double context, not a newly specified numerical cutoff. Two-hand triples use broad span 0–48; no mandatory wide minimum is invented. Melodic doubles ascend or descend where assigned, and other melodic examples use random played order. Physical hand placement, comfortable reach, fingering and instrument technique are not assessed or simulated.

Transposing-instrument assignments use written note names that need not match concert black-key pitches. An instrument-specific written/concert offset is not implemented; follow the retained source instructions with an appropriate instrument and partner, not an assumed concert-pitch formula. Manual acknowledgement is not verification. The A-based guitar team five-tone pool remains unresolved: no C-major or A-major complement is guessed, no formula is generated, and deferred acknowledgement confers no mastery.

The D-string cue [50] is synthesized, not a real-string recording. F#-major [54,58,61], G#-major [56,60,63] and A#-major [58,62,65] are close-position app major-triad voicings; A#, B# and C## may appear under enharmonic keyboard names. These are not copied old minor voicings or source-prescribed guitar fingerings. Cue → target repeats for every trial, with two separately tracked rounds of twenty inherited from earlier work, not explicitly restated. Other formulas retain source round counts: one for solo and team melodic work, two for team harmonic doubles/triples. Errors reset the current twenty-correct round. Harmonic naming is bottom-up with reordering allowed before a wrong-order error.

Source status: text_supported_audio_unverified. Source windows and quotes are evidence references, not independently verified audio. MIDI 36–84, random sampling, synthesized playback and keyboard entry are app adaptations, not source timing, distribution, register or voicing requirements. Distinct excludes exact repeated MIDI notes but permits octave duplicates; source repeat policy is unspecified. Simultaneous-tone assignments require an appropriate instrument; the continued single-tone-instrument accommodation permits omitting harmonic examples. Digital playback does not establish physical one-/two-hand technique or a universal hand-span model.

Complete 2 separately tracked round(s) of twenty consecutive correct examples; an error resets the current round. Name bottom-up; correct pitch classes in the wrong order may be reordered after a hint. App adaptation: MIDI 36–84 is a finite synthesized playback range, not a source-assigned register or octave-specific vocal requirement. App adaptation: synthesized playback and keyboard note-name entry replace instrument/partner actions; naming is listening and naming, not singing. App adaptation: distinct selects different absolute MIDI notes, allows octave duplicates of pitch classes, and excludes exact repeated notes within an example. Source repeat-note policy and randomization distribution are unspecified. App adaptation: physical one-/two-hand placement, fingering, hand reach and guitar technique are not assessed or simulated. A numeric span does not guarantee an individual can physically play an example; use a comfortable reach on the real instrument. App adaptation: sequential examples are answered in played order; unspecified melodic ordering is sampled randomly. Simultaneous harmonic examples are named bottom-up. App adaptation: allow a right-pitch-classes/wrong-order hint and reordering before marking an error; harmonic naming still requires bottom-up order (master-class-09 segments 3–8).

practices.title: Five-tone singles — team players — transposing instruments
practices.description: Identify newly studied pitches with a partner. Continue the established singles, doubles, and triples with the newly assigned five-tone collection. Manual instrument/partner guidance only: use the source written names C#, F#, Eb, Ab, Bb for your transposing instrument. Determine the actual written/concert offset for that instrument before practising; this app does not implement instrument-specific transposition or automatically check the result. Follow the source presentation, correction and continued round criterion on the physical instrument. Acknowledge only that you reviewed/practised this guidance; acknowledgement is not verification, a passed round or mastery.

practices.text: All ten source activities are individually exposed (p01–p10 → numeric 2–11). Six entries provide interactive MEDITATION_GUIDE sessions: p02, p03, p05, p06, p07 and p09. Four GUIDED_PRACTICE entries remain manual: the instructor-only demonstration, physical guitar, flexible chord adaptations and normal instrument practice. All controls are learner-paced: no automatic reference playback, silence deadline, compulsory repetition count, microphone grading, cents tolerance, accuracy target or verification rounds. Play/check only when requested. App MIDI 48–84 and the default register are adaptations, not source requirements. Use your own instrument when appropriate; a transposing-instrument C need not be concert C. Session logging is not mastery. Bottom-anchor sets include the octave and finish on the lower anchor, without a compulsory set count. The top-anchor 12-semitone window is an app choice, not a source lower endpoint. First recall never auto-plays its reference; later random recall preserves self-selected named-note controls with randomness optional. All source metadata remains text_supported_audio_unverified; quotes/windows are not independently verified audio.

practices.description: Recall and compare individual pitch qualities. Begin on white notes; gently listen and imagine C, D, E and the other notes. Interactive keyboard guidance offers named white, black and mixed collections in that order. White pitch classes are 0,2,4,5,7,9,11; black are 1,3,6,8,10; mixed contains all twelve. The learner chooses when familiarity warrants changing stage, chooses named notes, imagines/sings and requests a check. C→G→B is illustrative, not a compulsory route. No stage accuracy gate is invented.

practices.title: Random inner recall with progressively fewer checks
practices.description: Confident mental pitch recall without constant prompts. As proficiency develops, move among notes at random; D, G#, B, C# are examples. Interactive later-stage recall uses self-selected named notes, not a mandatory generic random prompt. Named note controls let the learner choose any available pitch; an optional random-selection button is only a user-requested convenience. No reference sounds automatically before imagination/singing. Check when doubtful; reduce checks only with subjective confidence, never suppress needed checking or remove all checks through a score threshold. D, G#, B and C# are examples, not a fixed pool.

practices.text: Twelve source activities become twenty activity entries plus player/comments (22 total): sixteen formula drills, two reference-pattern drills, one mixed-pattern drill and one manual guidance entry. Source p01–p12 map to numeric 2–13; p11/p12 singles stay at 12/13 and their extra forms use 14–17/18–21. Each entry has a unique stable practice_uid; source_practice_id remains provenance and repeats across team forms. Black/white counting credits successful five-tone patterns: ten per round, three rounds, not 150 tone hits and not an invented consecutive-pattern rule. An error discards only the current pattern as an explicit app policy; the source does not specify loss of prior counts. Reference blocks have six targets, while the alternating extra-target cycle has eight; both remain open without score gates. Meditation remains open recall. Team forms preserve the full scale-plus-added-tone pools; harmonic doubles/triples have two rounds and other forms one. Twenty-example sizes where unstated, consecutiveness/reset behavior, MIDI 36–84, random sampling, cue registers and app form organization are disclosed adaptations/inherited conventions, not fresh source prescriptions. Guitar team A-major/F-natural transposition remains qualified by the source uncertainty. Review status is text_supported_audio_unverified; windows/quotes have not been independently audio-verified. Continue daily without forcing pitch color; optional twice-daily work must not tire the ear or replace the next day’s session. No guarantees of perfect pitch are validated by the app.

practices.skill: Practice readiness
source_instructions: Be properly rested and alert rather than half falling asleep during ear training.
The instructor also encourages nourishment, exercise, recreation, relaxation and meditation as whole-musician support, without a prescribed regimen.
practices.presentation: Preparation for ordinary practice, not a note-identification trial.
practices.response: Approach practice alert; no response is scored.

evidence.quote: We have to be properly rested.
I said earlier, if you want to practice best,
you have to be alert.
You can't sit there and be half falling asleep
and expect that you're going to train your ear
because the ear just won't hear if it's sleepy.
We have to be properly nourished.
We have to have proper exercise, proper recreation, relaxation, meditation, anything that helps
in improving the awareness of the musician as a whole will improve the awareness of pitch,
the awareness of musical processes, and everything that has to do with music.

carry_forward.instruction: Keep sessions short rather than doing ear training all day; then move on to instrument practice. Do not compulsively seek every A flat or identify every tone outside sessions.

evidence.quote: This may take you a little bit more listening to pass this drill. We don't
want to do ear training all day. We just take our short sessions. It's better. And
don't try to listen to everything outside of our ear training session. When
you go out into your daily activities, don't try to listen for all the A-flats
everywhere. Now sometimes we can listen, but if we can't hear it, we don't become
is all he'd talk about so the point is we don't want to overdo our ear training there's a time
and place for everything we take a small section of our day just a few minutes and we do these
drills and then we move on with our practicing of our instrument this is the important thing
And don't get yourself dizzy by trying to identify every tone and every piece you hear and all of this.

carry_forward.instruction: Hear what you can hear and be happy; do not mind what is not yet heard. Continue systematically and without forcing.

evidence.quote: Just keep doing your ear training. Just keep listening.
And remember this rule. Hear what you can hear and be happy about it.
And what you can't hear, don't mind. Just keep listening and keep improving in a very systematic, laid-back way.

practices.description: Source mapping and app adaptations.
practices.text: Thirteen source groups become 41 activity entries plus player/comments (43 entries, numeric IDs 0–42): 38 formula entries and three manual partner guidance entries. Source p01–p13 retain base IDs 2–14, including p13 at 14. Extra IDs 15–19 are white-root E/F/G/A/B; 20–23 black-root E-flat/F-sharp/A-flat/B-flat; 24–34 guitar G/E/C/B/F/B-flat/C-sharp/E-flat/F-sharp/A-flat/A; 35–38 and 39–42 are the four extra team forms for standard/guitar. Source IDs group variants; practice_uid uniquely identifies each selectable activity. White/black describes chord roots, never chord-note content. Major triads are cue_midi only, not target answers. Keyboard chord verification uses the disclosed inherited one-round twenty-consecutive convention; its count/reset is not restated here. Guitar chord and G/B/E reference sessions remain open without invented per-chord quotas. Guitar starts D, G, E, C; the remaining eight roots are an app listing order, not a source-required sequence. High E at MIDI 64 is an app voicing; the source leaves which E string ambiguous. Meditation doubles are open recall with sequential checking by default and optional simultaneous checking; the source does not choose melodic versus harmonic. Restricted team forms use only D/F/A-flat-or-G-sharp/B, one app round each including harmonic forms, without silently inheriting the earlier two-round rule; harmonic scope remains qualified by source uncertainty. Round size and reset are inherited app conventions. Speed recognition and grounding require an actual partner and remain manual: no BPM, time/accuracy quota or new turn rules. Keep sessions short, avoid prolonged diminished-pattern listening, ground with the familiar scale, and do not compulsively identify every daily-life tone. Source review is text_supported_audio_unverified, not an audio-verification claim.

source_instructions: Start with D major followed by any two tones, returning to D major between pairs.
Then complete G major, E major, C major, and all remaining major roots in any order.
Every chromatic tone is to serve as a major-chord root; complete these before the string drills.

practices.presentation: Fixed major chord, target, target; repeat for each root.

evidence.quote: this diminished seventh pattern. Now when you can do this drill quite well, then I'd like you to do
speed recognition of tones with the same drill. That means your partner plays

the note is. If he or she knows, they say the answer. If you don't know, then you
just let that note slip by. The point is to see if you can do it with speed

speed recognition without having to spend a lot of time to think about what that tone is. This is a good thing to do with all of our drills. in all your drills to go at a faster, even pace, simply playing notes. If you get it,
great. If you don't get it, just keep going. This speed recognition of tones will gear
up your ear to hear rapidly. It's a very good drill to do.

evidence.quote: a very good procedure if you ever have a doubt it's a choice between two notes then don't be
afraid say up or down and if you still don't know say up again you can go up up up as much as you

tones, then work with those two tones a little bit more. You'll get to know the difference.

You have to be your own ear trainer. And wherever you're finding a little weakness, a little
polishing needs to be done, then take that area up and polish that area.

practices.skill: Resolve pitch-name uncertainty through surrounding colors
source_instructions: If unsure between note names, say “up” or “down”; the tester plays a half step up or down.
Listen to the surrounding tones and judge the original uncertain tone.
If still unsure, request further up or down steps as much as desired.
practices.presentation: A doubtful target followed by tester-provided neighboring semitone steps on request.
practices.response: Request up/down; evaluate and identify the uncertain note.
practices.correction: Use additional neighboring tones as an aid; no penalty or maximum number of hints is imposed.

evidence.quote: If the person listening is not sure of what a tone is,
well, it's either a G or an A flat, and I don't know what it is.
Then what he can say is, up.
He tells the tester up, and the tester will then play up a half step.
And then the person listening says, well, if that had been a G, now it should be an A-flat.
Or maybe he'll say down, and the tester will go down a half step.
And oftentimes, this will give the listener a final judgment as to what it is.
When he hears the one note, he's not sure if it's G or A-flat.
but when you go up or down then he can make a very final judgment he's he's sure then this is
a very good procedure if you ever have a doubt it's a choice between two notes then don't be
afraid say up or down and if you still don't know say up again you can go up up up as much as you
want or down down down as much as you want in order to listen to the surrounding notes to make
make your evaluation. This is fine because this is all the development of this color
hearing, comparing the surrounding notes.

source_instructions: If the same two tones keep being confused, spend a little more work and careful listening on those two tones.
Find the weak area and polish it according to what your own ear needs; E flat/A flat and C sharp/F sharp are examples, not mandatory restricted pairs.

practices.presentation: Extra attentive listening to the two problem tones; no fixed alternation or randomization method is prescribed.
practices.response: Learn to distinguish the pair and improve the weak area.

evidence.quote: didn't think I could possibly make a mistake so I went home and I worked on these two I listened
to them a little bit more carefully so that I could hear the difference between the E flat and
the A flat. So if you're having an experience like this where sometimes you confuse two of the notes
like the C sharp and the F sharp because they have a little bit of a similar sound in some ways.
It's a very subjective thing. So if you ever have this experience where you're confusing two
tones, then work with those two tones a little bit more. You'll get to know the difference.
See, at this point you'll have to see what your own ear needs. We don't have a recipe.
You have to be your own ear trainer. And wherever you're finding a little weakness, a little
polishing needs to be done, then take that area up and polish that area.
